evidence.positive: Exercised the real MGB notification surface on the running app (unauthenticated POST /api/integration/mgh/event, tenant mgb-mgh via the HOSPITAL=MGH entity, payload = the shipped mgb-notification-models IN_ROOM.xml with the User ID swapped). Seeded a stale practitioner (epic_user_id DEDUPBASE1, last_refreshed_at NULL) and fired 6 simultaneous notifications naming it. Log shows all 6 request threads found it stale ('Practitioner DEDUPBASE1 has never been refreshed, triggering refresh' x6), exactly ONE won the claim, and 5 logged 'Skipping refresh for practitioner DEDUPBASE1 - a refresh is already in flight'. Only ONE outbound Epic call resulted: a single 'Searching practitioners by name: https://stage-webapi.partners.org/TST/api/FHIR/PHSFHIR/R4/Practitioner?name=BASE+SETUP' on thread practitioner-refresh-1. Valkey held exactly one claim key while in flight: tenant/mgb-mgh/practitioner/<uuid>/refreshInFlight with TTL 4 (of the 5s window). Repeated after the class restore (DEDUPRESTORE1): 6 messages -> 6 stale triggers, 5 skips, 1 Epic lookup at 20:58:23.977Z.
evidence.negative: Two inverse cases. (1) Claim does not suppress a different practitioner: fired 4+4 simultaneous notifications naming two distinct stale practitioners (DEDUPNEGA1 / DEDUPNEGB1). Each id logged 4 stale triggers and 3 skips, and exactly two Epic lookups ran, one per id ('name=ALPHA+NEGA' on practitioner-refresh-3, 'name=BRAVO+NEGB' on practitioner-refresh-2). Valkey showed two separate keys whose UUIDs matched each practitioner row (25909e17... for NEGA, 27dfaf57... for NEGB), so the claim is per-tenant-per-practitioner. (2) A non-stale practitioner is neither refreshed nor charged a Redis round trip: set DEDUPFRESH1.last_refreshed_at = now(), deleted any leftover key, fired 4 concurrent notifications -> zero staleness-trigger lines, zero 'already in flight' lines, zero 'Searching practitioners by name' lines, and 'keys *refreshInFlight*' returned empty. Also exercised the fail-open branch at runtime: stopped the valkey container and fired 3 concurrent notifications for DEDUPNOREDIS1 -> 3x WARN 'Could not claim the refresh window for practitioner DEDUPNOREDIS1 - refreshing anyway' and all 3 refreshes ran, so a Redis outage does not silently disable practitioner refresh.
evidence.red_check: Ran the pre-fix code in the container. Extracted PractitionerService.java from the parent commit (5f0618aad^), replaced @Slf4j with an explicit slf4j logger (lombok is not on the runtime classpath) and added one WARN marker at each refresh trigger carrying a per-epic-user-id counter, compiled it in-container with javac against /app/classes:/app/libs/*, backed up the shipped class (md5 4785a9ad9bea099250cf379c92dc3e2b, copied to scratch as well), swapped in the pre-fix class (md5 4a589eb486ff75c561a2d6dc9a613698) and restarted the app (Started OrciApplication at 20:54:50). Fired the same 6 simultaneous notifications for a fresh stale practitioner REDDUP2797. The check went red: SIX refresh triggers for the one practitioner ('PREFIX-BUILD refresh trigger number 1..6 for practitioner REDDUP2797', all at 20:55:17.905Z), ZERO 'a refresh is already in flight' lines, NO refreshInFlight key in valkey, and 4 duplicate concurrent Epic Practitioner searches for 'name=RHO+REDCHK' at 20:55:18.11Z (core pool is 4; the other 2 queued) instead of 1. Then restored: copied the backup back, md5 re-verified as 4785a9ad9bea099250cf379c92dc3e2b, restarted (Started OrciApplication at 20:56:15), and re-ran the positive case -> 6 triggers, 5 skips, 1 Epic lookup, zero PREFIX-BUILD lines. Instance left running the shipped class.

red_check_signature: PREFIX-BUILD refresh trigger number 6 for practitioner REDDUP2797
caveats: The merged change does not fix the Sentry HTTP 500 the ticket was opened from; the commit says so explicitly (upstream Epic failure, 2 of 1404 lookups). If the ticket is meant to close that Sentry issue rather than the duplicate-lookup volume behind it, the issue can recur.

Validated through the MGB notification endpoint on mgb-mgh; the Mayo HL7 caller (DefaultHL7ProcessingContext.resolvePractitioner) reaches the same PractitionerService method and was not exercised separately.

Epic is unreachable from this instance, so every refresh ended in a 30s connect timeout. That is longer than the 5s claim window, so messages arriving more than 5s into an in-flight lookup do start a second one — visible in this environment, not in prod where the lookup is sub-second, but it means dedup is weakest exactly during an Epic outage.
The pre-fix class was recompiled with an explicit logger and one added counter/marker log line, since lombok is absent at runtime; the dedup logic itself was the parent commit's verbatim.
Practitioner rows for the negative and red-check cases were inserted with SQL rather than created through a first notification, to avoid an extra 30s FHIR timeout per setup.

automation.assessment: Coverage is already good and no gap is worth filling. The fix commit added five unit tests in PractitionerServiceTest covering the lost-claim skip (and that the caller still gets the practitioner), tenant+practitioner key scoping, claim-window bounds, the Redis-failure fail-open, and that a non-stale practitioner costs no Redis call. RedisServiceTest already proves setValueIfAbsent is atomic under concurrency against a real Redis, which is the primitive this fix rests on. An end-to-end concurrency test through the notification endpoint would add flake for behavior the runtime validation above already demonstrated.

jira_comment:
Verdict: deploy-ready.

Positive: Six simultaneous MGB notifications naming one stale practitioner produced a single Epic Practitioner lookup, five skip-because-in-flight log lines, and one per-practitioner claim key in Valkey with a 5 second window.
Negative: Two different stale practitioners hit concurrently each got their own lookup with no cross-suppression, a practitioner refreshed a moment ago triggered no lookup and no Redis call at all, and with Valkey stopped every message refreshed anyway rather than refresh being silently disabled.
Red check: The parent commit's PractitionerService was compiled and swapped into the running container, after which the same six messages triggered six refreshes and four concurrent duplicate Epic lookups with no skip lines; the shipped class was restored, checksum verified, and the positive case re-ran clean.

Automation: The fix commit's unit tests plus the existing atomic-claim coverage are sufficient, so no new tests are proposed.

Note: this does not address the HTTP 500 in the Sentry issue itself, which the commit calls an upstream Epic failure.
